problem.summary: 现有动作识别数据集（如UCF-101和HMDB-51）规模过小，导致难以区分不同视频架构的性能优劣，且现有模型在小规模基准上表现相似。

motivation.summary: 需要一个大规模、真实且具有挑战性的视频数据集来重新评估现有架构，并探索视频预训练对动作识别任务的价值。

core_idea.summary: 提出一个新的大规模Kinetics数据集，并引入一种新的Two-Stream Inflated 3D ConvNet (I3D)模型，该模型通过将成功的2D图像分类网络（如Inception-v1）的滤波器和池化核扩展到3D，从而利用ImageNet架构设计和参数，学习无缝的时空特征提取器。

method.summary: 1. 构建Kinetics数据集（400类，每类400+片段）。2. 重新实现并评估多种现有架构（ConvNet+LSTM, 3D-ConvNet, Two-Stream, 3D-Fused）。3. 提出I3D模型：通过将2D滤波器和池化核“膨胀”为3D，并采用双流配置（RGB和光流）。4. 在Kinetics上预训练I3D模型，然后在UCF-101和HMDB-51上微调。

experiments.summary: 在UCF-101、HMDB-51和Kinetics数据集上，对比了五种架构的性能。评估了预训练策略（ImageNet预训练、Kinetics预训练、两者结合）的效果。将I3D模型与当时最先进的方法进行了比较。

claims.claim: 大规模视频数据集（Kinetics）对于区分和改进视频架构至关重要。
提出的I3D模型在动作识别任务上达到了新的最优性能。
在Kinetics上进行视频预训练能显著提升模型在UCF-101和HMDB-51上的性能。
将2D ConvNet膨胀为3D是构建有效时空特征提取器的有效方法。
双流配置（RGB + 光流）对I3D模型性能仍有显著贡献。

limitations.limitation: 论文未对架构进行全面探索（如不同膨胀策略、更多2D架构）。未验证Kinetics预训练对其他视频任务（如语义分割、目标检测）的迁移效果。光流计算（TV-L1）可能成为瓶颈。

nodes.title: Kinetics数据集构建
nodes.label: 数据准备
nodes.summary: 构建了一个大规模、真实的人类动作视频数据集，用于模型预训练和评估。
nodes.description: Kinetics数据集包含400个人类动作类别，每个类别有超过400个来自不同YouTube视频的片段，总训练视频约24万。片段时长约10秒，无未修剪视频。测试集每类100个片段。

nodes.title: 现有架构重新实现与评估
nodes.label: 基线模型
nodes.summary: 重新实现了多种代表性的视频分类神经网络架构，作为性能比较的基线。
nodes.description: 重新实现的架构包括：ConvNet+LSTM、3D-ConvNet（C3D变体）、Two-Stream、3D-Fused。这些模型基于ImageNet预训练的Inception-v1（除3D-ConvNet从头训练外），并在不同数据集上训练和测试。

nodes.title: 2D ConvNet膨胀为3D
nodes.label: 核心创新
nodes.summary: 提出将成功的2D图像分类网络（如Inception-v1）的滤波器和池化核扩展一个时间维度，从而构建3D ConvNet。
nodes.description: 膨胀操作：将2D滤波器（如k×k）扩展为3D滤波器（如t×k×k），并复制2D权重沿时间维度初始化。这使得网络能够利用ImageNet预训练的参数和架构设计。同时考虑了“无聊视频”固定点和感受野增长的节奏。

nodes.title: Two-Stream Inflated 3D ConvNet (I3D)
nodes.label: 提出模型
nodes.summary: 结合双流思想和膨胀3D ConvNet，提出I3D模型，包含RGB流和光流两个分支。
nodes.description: I3D模型基于膨胀的Inception-v1架构。采用双流配置：一个I3D网络处理RGB输入，另一个处理光流输入。训练时使用64帧片段，测试时对整个视频进行卷积预测并平均。模型参数约25M。

nodes.title: 预训练与微调策略
nodes.label: 训练流程
nodes.summary: 探索了不同的预训练策略：ImageNet预训练、Kinetics预训练、两者结合，然后在目标数据集上微调。
nodes.description: 模型首先在ImageNet上预训练（可选），然后在Kinetics上训练110k步。之后，在UCF-101/HMDB-51上进行微调（最多5k步）。评估了固定特征（仅训练最后一层）和完全微调两种方式。

nodes.title: 实验评估与比较
nodes.label: 实验分析
nodes.summary: 在多个数据集上系统评估了不同架构和预训练策略，并与当时最先进的方法进行了比较。
nodes.description: 实验包括：1) 在UCF-101、HMDB-51、Kinetics上直接训练测试各架构（表2）。2) 评估ImageNet预训练对Kinetics训练的影响（表3）。3) 评估Kinetics预训练对UCF-101/HMDB-51性能的影响（表4）。4) 与state-of-the-art方法比较（表5）。

edges.label: 提供评估平台
edges.description: Kinetics数据集为重新实现和评估现有架构提供了大规模、有挑战性的基准。

edges.label: 用于预训练
edges.description: Kinetics数据集用于预训练提出的I3D模型，以学习通用的时空特征。

edges.label: 作为比较基线
edges.description: 重新实现的现有架构的性能结果，为评估新模型（I3D）提供了基线。

edges.label: 构建基础
edges.description: 2D ConvNet膨胀技术是构建I3D模型中3D卷积层的核心方法。

edges.label: 接受训练
edges.description: I3D模型按照预训练与微调策略进行训练。

edges.label: 产生结果
edges.description: 经过不同预训练和微调策略训练的模型，在实验评估中产生性能结果。

deltas.before: Two-Stream ConvNet：使用2D ConvNet（如Inception-v1）独立处理视频中采样的单个帧，然后平均预测。忽略了时间结构。
deltas.after: I3D：将2D ConvNet的滤波器和池化核膨胀为3D，使其能够直接处理视频片段（如64帧），学习时空特征。
deltas.why_it_matters: 使模型能够捕捉帧间的时间动态和运动信息，而不仅仅是静态外观，这对于区分动作（如开门与关门）至关重要。

deltas.before: C3D：使用从头训练的浅层3D ConvNet（8层卷积），参数较多（79M），且无法利用ImageNet预训练。
deltas.after: I3D：基于更深的2D架构（Inception-v1）膨胀而来，参数更少（25M），并能利用ImageNet预训练的权重进行初始化。
deltas.why_it_matters: 更深的架构和ImageNet预训练带来了更强的特征表示能力，同时参数效率更高，训练更稳定。

deltas.before: 现有模型在小数据集（UCF-101, HMDB-51）上性能饱和，难以区分优劣。
deltas.after: 在Kinetics大数据集上预训练后，I3D模型在UCF-101和HMDB-51上取得了显著的性能提升（例如，UCF-101从94.2%提升到98.0%）。
deltas.why_it_matters: 证明了大规模视频预训练的价值，并确立了新的性能基准，推动了领域发展。

formulas.latex: \text{I3D滤波器尺寸} = t \times k \times k \quad (\text{从} k \times k \text{膨胀而来})

variables.name: t
variables.description: 时间维度大小（膨胀因子）

variables.name: k
variables.description: 空间维度大小（来自原始2D滤波器）

formulas.intuition: 将2D空间滤波器在时间维度上进行复制扩展，使其能够处理视频序列。这是构建I3D模型的核心操作。

variables.name: T
variables.description: 测试时视频被分割成的片段数量

variables.name: f_{\text{I3D}}
variables.description: I3D模型对单个视频片段的预测函数

formulas.intuition: 在测试阶段，将整个视频分割成多个片段，分别用I3D模型进行预测，然后对所有片段的预测结果取平均，得到最终的视频级分类结果。

在Kinetics上预训练后，所有模型在UCF-101/HMDB-51上的性能都得到提升，但提升幅度因架构而异。

risk_flags: 性能比较基于特定数据集（UCF-101, HMDB-51）和评估协议（split 1）。当时最优性能可能随时间被超越。

evidence.description: 在UCF-101和HMDB-51数据集上，经过ImageNet和Kinetics预训练的Two-Stream I3D模型达到了当时最优性能（UCF-101: 98.0%, HMDB-51: 80.7%）。

claims.claim: 在Kinetics上进行视频预训练能显著提升模型在UCF-101和HMDB-51上的性能。
risk_flags: 提升幅度因架构和目标数据集而异。未验证对更广泛视频理解任务的迁移效果。

evidence.description: 评估了不同预训练策略（ImageNet、Kinetics、两者结合）以及固定特征与完全微调的影响。Kinetics预训练比ImageNet预训练带来更大提升。

claims.claim: 将2D ConvNet膨胀为3D是构建有效时空特征提取器的有效方法。

论文指出，虽然3D ConvNet应能从RGB输入直接学习运动特征，但实验表明双流配置仍有价值。

terms.definition: 本文提出的大规模人类动作视频数据集，包含400个类别，每类超过400个片段，总训练视频约24万。
本文提出的模型，通过将2D ConvNet（如Inception-v1）的滤波器和池化核膨胀到3D，并采用双流配置（RGB和光流）来处理视频。
将2D卷积滤波器或池化核扩展一个时间维度（例如，从k×k变为t×k×k）的操作，通常使用2D权重沿时间维度复制进行初始化。
一种视频分类架构范式，使用两个独立的网络分支分别处理RGB图像和光流图像，然后融合它们的预测。

terms.term: 无聊视频固定点 (Boring Video Fixed Point)
terms.definition: 一个设计原则，指对于内容不变（如静态场景）的视频，网络的输出应保持不变。这指导了膨胀操作中非线性层和池化层的设计。
在大型数据集（如ImageNet或Kinetics）上训练模型以学习通用特征表示，然后将其用于初始化下游任务模型的过程。
在预训练模型的基础上，使用目标任务的数据集（如UCF-101）对模型进行进一步训练，以适应特定任务。

steps.description: 1. 获取并预处理数据集：下载Kinetics、UCF-101、HMDB-51视频，并提取光流（使用TV-L1算法）。
2. 准备基础模型：获取在ImageNet上预训练的Inception-v1模型权重。
3. 实现I3D模型：根据论文描述（图3）实现膨胀的Inception-v1架构，包括双流配置。
4. 在Kinetics上预训练：使用64帧片段、随机裁剪等数据增强，在Kinetics上训练I3D模型约110k步。
5. 在目标数据集上微调：使用预训练的I3D模型，在UCF-101或HMDB-51上进行微调（最多5k步）。
6. 评估：在测试集上评估模型，采用对整个视频进行卷积预测并平均的策略。

metadata.title: Quo Vadis, Action Recognition? A New Model and the Kinetics Dataset
metadata.paper_type: Computer Vision / Video Understanding / Computer Vision / Top-cited Computer Vision paper
metadata.abstract: The paucity of videos in current action classification datasets (UCF-101 and HMDB-51) has made it difficult to identify good video architectures, as most methods obtain similar performance on existing small-scale benchmarks. This paper re-evaluates state-of-the-art architectures in light of the new Kinetics Human Action Video dataset. Kinetics has two orders of magnitude more data, with 400 human action classes and over 400 clips per class, and is collected from realistic, challenging YouTube videos. We provide an analysis on how current architectures fare on the task of action classification on this dataset and how much performance improves on the smaller benchmark datasets after pre-training on Kinetics. We also introduce a new Two-Stream Inflated 3D ConvNet (I3D) that is based on 2D ConvNet inflation: filters and pooling kernels of very deep image classification ConvNets are expanded into 3D, making it possible to learn seamless spatio-temporal feature extractors from video while leveraging successful ImageNet architecture designs and even their parameters. We show that, after pre-training on Kinetics, I3D models considerably improve upon the state-of-the-art in action classification, reaching 80.2% on HMDB-51 and 97.9% on UCF-101.

The paucity of videos in current action classiﬁcation datasets (UCF-101 and HMDB-51) has made it difﬁcult to identify good video architectures, as most methods ob- tain similar performance on existing small-scale bench- marks. This paper re-evaluates state-of-the-art architec- tures in light of the new Kinetics Human Action Video dataset. Kinetics has two orders of magnitude more data, with 400 human action classes and over 400 clips per class, and is collected from realistic, challenging YouTube videos. We provide an analysis on how current architectures fare on the task of action classiﬁcation on this dataset and how much performance improves on the smaller benchmark datasets after pre-training on Kinetics. We also introduce a new Two-Stream Inﬂated 3D Con- vNet (I3D) that is based on 2D ConvNet inﬂation: ﬁl- ters and pooling kernels of very deep image classiﬁca- tion ConvNets are expanded into 3D, making it possible to learn seamless spatio-temporal feature extractors from video wh...
Figure 1. A still from ‘Quo Vadis’ (1951). Where is this going?
Are these actors about to kiss each other, or have they just done so? More importantly, where is action recognition going? Actions can be ambiguous in individual frames, but the limitations of exist-
ing action recognition datasets has meant that the best-performing

video architectures do not depart signiﬁcantly from single-image analysis, where they rely on powerful image classiﬁers trained on ImageNet. In this paper we demonstrate that video models are best pre-trained on videos and report signiﬁcant improvements by using spatio-temporal classiﬁers pre-trained on Kinetics, a freshly
collected, large, challenging human action video dataset.

ing an action classiﬁcation network on a sufﬁciently large

dataset, will give a similar boost in performance when ap- plied to a different temporal task or dataset. The chal- lenges of building video datasets has meant that most popu- lar benchmarks for action recognition are small, having on the order of 10k videos. In this paper we aim to provide an answer to this question using the new Kinetics Human Action Video Dataset [16],
which is two orders of magnitude larger than previous
datasets, HMDB-51 [18] and UCF-101 [29]. Kinetics has 1 arXiv:1705.07750v3 [cs.CV] 12 Feb 2018

400 human action classes with more than 400 examples for each class, each from a unique YouTube video. Our experimental strategy is to reimplement a number of representative neural network architectures from the litera- ture, and then analyze their transfer behavior by ﬁrst pre- training each one on Kinetics and then ﬁne-tuning each on HMDB-51 and UCF-101. The results suggest that there is always a boost in performance by pre-training, but the ex- tent of the boost varies signiﬁcantly with the type of archi- tecture. Based on these ﬁndings, we introduce a new model that has the capacity to take advantage of pre-training on Kinetics, and can achieves a high performance. The model termed a “Two-Stream Inﬂated 3D ConvNets” (I3D), builds upon state-of-the-art image classiﬁcation architectures, but inﬂates their ﬁlters and pooling kernels (and optionally their parameters) into 3D, leading to very deep, naturally spatio- temporal classiﬁers. change as possible for video. This can be achieved by using them to extract features independently from each frame then pooling their predictions across the whole video [15]. This is in the spirit of bag of words image modeling approaches [19, 22, 33]; but while convenient in practice, it has the issue of entirely ignoring temporal structure (e.g. models can’t potentially distinguish opening from closing a door). In theory, a more satisfying approach is to add a recur- rent layer to the model [5, 37], such as an LSTM, which can encode state, and capture temporal ordering and long range dependencies. We position an LSTM layer with batch nor- malization (as proposed by Cooijmans et al. [4]) after the last average pooling layer of Inception-V1, with 512 hid- den units. A fully connected layer is added on top for the classiﬁer. The model is trained using cross-entropy losses on the outputs at all time steps. During testing we consider only the output on the last frame. Input video frames...

Also, they seem to preclude the beneﬁts of ImageNet pre-training, and consequently previous work has deﬁned relatively shallow custom archi- tectures and trained them from scratch [14, 15, 30, 31]. Re- sults on benchmarks have shown promise but have not been competitive with state-of-the-art, making this type of mod-
els a good candidate for evaluation on our larger dataset.

For this paper we implemented a small variation of C3D [31], which has 8 convolutional layers, 5 pooling layers and 2 fully connected layers at the top. The inputs to the model are short 16-frame clips with 112 × 112-pixel crops as in the original implementation. Differently from [31] we used batch normalization after all convolutional and fully con- nected layers. Another difference to the original model is in the ﬁrst pooling layer, we use a temporal stride of 2 in- stead of 1, which reduces the memory footprint and allows for bigger batches – this was important for batch normal- ization (especially after the fully connected layers, where there is no weight tying). Using this stride we were able to train with 15 videos per batch per GPU using standard K40 GPUs. 2.3. The New: Two-Stream Inﬂated 3D ConvNets With this architecture, we show how 3D ConvNets can beneﬁt from ImageNet 2D ConvNet designs and, option- ally, from their learned parameters. We also adopt a two- stream conﬁguration here – it will be shown in section 4

that while 3D ConvNets can directly learn about temporal patterns from an RGB stream, their performance can still be greatly improved by including an optical-ﬂow stream. Inﬂating 2D ConvNets into 3D.A number of very success- ful image classiﬁcation architectures have been developed over the years, in part through painstaking trial and error. Instead of repeating the process for spatio-temporal models we propose to simply convert successful image (2D) clas- siﬁcation models into 3D ConvNets. This can be done by starting with a 2D architecture, and inﬂating all the ﬁlters and pooling kernels – endowing them with an additional temporal dimension. Filters are typically square and we just make them cubic – N × N ﬁlters become N × N × N. Bootstrapping 3D ﬁlters from 2D Filters. Pacing receptive ﬁeld growth in space, time and net- work depth. The boring video ﬁxed-point leaves ample freedom on how to inﬂate pooling operators along the time dimension and on how to set convolutional/pooling tempo- ral stride – these are the primary factors that shape the size of feature receptive ﬁelds. Virtually all image models treat the two spatial dimensions (horizontal and vertical) equally – pooling kernels and strides are the same. This is quite natural and means that features deeper in the networks are equally affected by image locations increasingly far away in both dimensions. A symmetric receptive ﬁeld is however not necessarily optimal when also considering time – this should depend on frame rate and image dimensions. The Kinetics Human Action Video Dataset The Kinetics dataset is focused on human actions (rather than activities or events). The list of action classes covers: Person Actions (singular) , e.g. drawing, drinking, laugh- ing, punching; Person-Person Actions, e.g. hugging, kiss- ing, shaking hands; and, Person-Object Actions, e.g. open- ing presents, mowing lawn, washing dishes. Some actions are ﬁne grained and require temporal reasoning to distin-
guish, for example different types of swimming. Other ac-

tions require more emphasis on the object to distinguish, for example playing different types of wind instruments. The dataset has 400 human action classes, with 400 or more clips for each class, each from a unique video, for a total of 240k training videos. The clips last around 10s, and there are no untrimmed videos. The test set consists of 100 clips for each class. A full description of the dataset and how it was built is given in [16]. 4. Discussion We return to the question posed in the introduction, “is there a beneﬁt in transfer learning from videos?”. It is evi- dent that there is a considerable beneﬁt in pre-training on
(the large video dataset) Kinetics, just as there has been

such beneﬁts in pre-training ConvNets on ImageNet for so many tasks. This demonstrates transfer learning from one dataset (Kinetics) to another dataset (UCF-101/HMDB-51) for a similar task (albeit for different action classes). How- ever, it still remains to be seen if there is a beneﬁt in using Kinetics pre-training for other video tasks such as seman- tic video segmentation, video object detection, or optical ﬂow computation. We plan to make publicly available I3D models trained on the ofﬁcial Kinetics dataset’s release to facilitate research in this area. Of course, we did not perform a comprehensive explo- ration of architectures – for example we have not employed action tubes [11, 17] or attention mechanisms [20] to fo- cus in on the human actors. Recent works have proposed
imaginative methods for determining the spatial and tem-
poral extent (detection) of actors within the two-stream architectures, by incorporating linked object detections in

time [24, 26]. The relationship between space and time is a mysterious one. Several very creative papers have recently gone out of the box in attempts to capture this relationship, for example by learning frame ranking functions for action classes and using these as a representation [9], by making
analogies between actions and transformations [36], or by

creating 2D visual snapshots of frame sequences [2] – this idea is related to the classic motion history work of [3]. It would be of great value to also include these models in our comparison but we could not, due to lack of time and space.
